notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 53. I ran out of searches before I could check several of the sites you listed, and I've said below which ones are missing.

**Introduction and title**
- Guzik (enduringword.com) says the title names the author, the audience and the tune or instrument. He calls the psalm "essentially a repetition of Psalm 14, with a few small modifications." He thinks it was probably reused to give Israel courage during a national crisis such as an invasion or siege. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- Spurgeon says "Mahalath" seems in some forms to mean "disease," so he reads the psalm as THE SONG OF MAN'S DISEASE— the mortal, hereditary taint of sin. URL: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps053.cfm
- Matthew Poole (quoted on Bible Hub) thinks David sang the psalm again for a new occasion with small changes. He says the compilers kept it out of reverence for David's inspired writings. He also says we should admit we don't know what "Mahalath" means rather than guess. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-1.htm
- The Bible Hub study notes say "Maskil" marks a teaching psalm. Just as Psalm 32 (also a Maskil) instructs on confession, Psalm 53 instructs on the folly of unbelief. URL: https://biblehub.com/psalms/53-1.htm

**v. 1**
- **What "fool" means.** Guzik says the word (*nabal*) is about morals more than intelligence. He quotes Kidner: it means "an aggressive perversity," as with Nabal in 1 Samuel 25:25. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- The Cambridge Bible agrees: "fool" describes a type of person, not one individual, and points to moral perversity rather than ignorance. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-1.htm
- **"There is no God."** Several commentators read this as practical atheism, not a philosophical denial.
  - Guzik, quoting Boice, says the Hebrew is literally "No God," meaning "No God for me." URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
  - The Cambridge Bible says This is not to be understood of a speculative denial of the existence of God; but of a practical denial of His moral government. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-1.htm
  - Gill says the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) adds "of whom is revenge," meaning no God who punishes the wicked. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-1.html
  - A quotation in Spurgeon disagrees on the grammar: it says the Hebrew cannot be explained as a wish—"No God!" URL: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps053.cfm
- **"In his heart."** Guzik says the person wishes God away for moral reasons. He adds that someone can believe in God in their head and still be a practical atheist in how they live. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- **"Corrupt… vile."** Spurgeon: "*No God*," being interpreted, means no law, no order, no restraint to lust, no limit to passion. URL: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps053.cfm
- Ellicott notes that Psalm 14 has the general word "doings," while Psalm 53 has the stronger "iniquity." URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-1.htm
- Everett notes that the Hebrew word for "corrupt" is the same one used of humanity before the Flood (Genesis 6:11–12). URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/psalms-53.html?print=yes
- **Catholic reading (Augustine).** Augustine says people who openly deny God are rare. But anyone who thinks God approves of their sin is really saying "There is no God," because a just God hates sin. He describes a downward path: corruption starts with wrong belief, moves to bad morals, then to open wickedness. URL: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801053.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik says people may forget God, but God never forgets them. He quotes Kidner, who compares this to God coming down at Babel and looking on the world before the Flood. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- Guzik also says God is not looking for clever people. He is looking for people who understand His heart and seek Him. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- Guzik notes that this psalm keeps using *Elohim* ("God") where Psalm 14 uses *Yahweh* ("the LORD"). He says the reason is hard to tell. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- Spurgeon says God was not looking for great holiness, but only for sincerity and right desire, but these he found not. (Treasury of David, on Bible Hub) URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-1.htm
- Augustine asks why an all-knowing God would need to "see." He says the words are spoken as if by someone asking a question, and then God delivers His verdict in v. 3. URL: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801053.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik quotes Poole: "turned aside" can mean "grown sour," like spoiled drink, and "become corrupt" is like rotten meat. He quotes Kidner: this verse widens the charge from the atheist of v. 1 to all of us. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- Spurgeon says Psalm 14 has "turned aside," but here people are going "back," that is, in the opposite direction. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-1.htm
- The Bible Hub study notes link this verse to total depravity and to Romans 3:10–12, where Paul quotes it. They say it points to the need for a Savior. URL: https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/53-1.htm
- A Lutheran resource on 1517.org (a short podcast song) sums up the theme: Everyone is stained by sin. URL: https://www.1517.org/scripture/psalm-53
- **Tradition note.** I couldn't find a Methodist or Wesleyan comment on this verse; Wesley's Notes on Psalm 53 only comment on v. 5. So I can't document a real Reformed-versus-Wesleyan disagreement here. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/53.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik says God's people may look like the weak fools, but it is the wicked who "have no knowledge." On "devour my people like bread," he quotes Poole: they do it with as little remorse as eating a meal. On "refuse to call upon God," he quotes Maclaren: practical atheism never prays. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
- Spurgeon: they may truly be said to know nothing that do not know God. URL: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps053.cfm
- Augustine says the people being "devoured" are those who have been made children of God, which is why the wicked prey on them. URL: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801053.htm

**v. 5** (This is where Psalm 53 differs most from Psalm 14.)
- **Whose fear is it?** Commentators disagree.
  - Guzik says the enemy will be terrified even though their position gave them nothing to fear. He gives examples of God doing this before: Gideon, Jonathan and Hezekiah. URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-53/
  - Spurgeon agrees: the attackers are seized with a causeless panic. URL: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps053.cfm
  - Barnes reads it the other way. He says the fear is that of God's people, and the psalmist is showing it was groundless because God had scattered the enemy. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-5.html
- **"Scattered the bones."** Barnes thinks the setting was a siege of Jerusalem that was driven off, with the enemy's bones left unburied. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-5.html
- Coffman says nothing is known about the actual event. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-5.html
- Benson mentions that many link it to Sheba's rebellion (2 Samuel 20). URL: https://studylight.org/commentaries/rbc/psalms-53.html
- **Methodist (Wesley).** "Scattered" means God both broke the enemy's strength and dispersed them, so as there is no hope of a restoration. In Wesley's reading, "thou" refers to Jerusalem under siege. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/53.htm
- **Baptist (Gill).** Gill applies the verse to the enemies of Christ and His church, and says God will destroy the antichrist and his armies. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-5.html
- **Catholic (Augustine).** Augustine gives a moral application: people fear losing money, where there is nothing truly to fear. But they don't fear losing wisdom, which really is something to fear. URL: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801053.htm
- The Douay-Rheims translation (from the Latin) reads "the bones of them that please men" instead of "those who besieged you." URL: https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/psalms/53-5.html

**v. 6**
- **Wording.** The Cambridge Bible prefers "restore the fortunes" over "bring back the captivity," so the verse need not mean the Exile. It also reads the last line as a prayer: "let Jacob rejoice." URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-6.htm
- Clarke says the Hebrew has "salvations" (plural) and is better translated as a question: "Who shall give…?" URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-6.html
- Barnes reads it as a longing for full freedom after the siege was lifted. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-6.htm
- **Where readings really differ is how far into the future this hope reaches:**
  - **Dispensational / Calvary Chapel:** Chuck Smith calls it a prayer for when Jesus comes to set up His kingdom. He says salvation from Zion always refers to Christ's millennial reign. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-6.html
  - Constable says that when Christ returns He will restore Israel as His favored nation. URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/53-6.html
  - **Baptist (Gill):** Gill reads it as the church freed from the antichrist's captivity, when both Gentiles are called and Jews converted. URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-6.htm
  - **Matthew Henry:** Henry reads it as salvation from sin, through the Redeemer named Jesus (Matthew 1:21). URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/53-6.htm
  - **Catholic (Augustine):** Augustine sees Christ here. The one the fools crucified, calling Him "no God," is the very one who brings salvation from Zion. Only He, who chose to become a captive in their hands, can end His people's captivity. URL: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801053.htm

**Not found**
- I didn't reach netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org, so there are no modern-scholarship notes. The closest I have is the Cambridge Bible's point about wording in v. 6.
- I found nothing from Orthodox (oca.org), Pentecostal, Lutheran (apart from the 1517 podcast line) or Anglican teachers on this psalm.
- I found no prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on Psalm 53.
- Note that Guzik and Chuck Smith both come from the Calvary Chapel movement, not a Pentecostal denomination.
